Dear all

I am a master student and fairly new to R and first time user of the unmarked package.

For my thesis I would like to obtain abundance and detection estimates using the pcount() function.

Here I got suspicious...so I estimated mean detection probabilities for each of the plots

> pred.obs.guentheri.table

Which resulted that I have an almost 100% detection rate in all of my 36 plots. 
Any advice how to deal with this? Earlier studies on this species estimated detection rates between 20 and 40%.
(I also tried to use ZIP instead of P, as there is quite some 0 in my data set, but I ended up with the same results)

What I found in an old post here, i think it was by Jim Baldwin, is that some data "barely obtain a unique maximum likelihood estimate". I am not sure if I used the provided code correctly but I run the first two bits of it

> mNull <- pcount(~1~1,UMF_guentheri, K=10000, control=list(reltol=0.0000000001))  #or K=100
> backTransform(mNull, type="state")
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Abundance estimate(s)

 Estimate   SE LinComb (Intercept)

Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Detection estimate(s)

 Estimate     SE LinComb (Intercept)
    0.234 0.0498   -1.18           1

Transformation: logistic 
> # Find correlation of the estimators of lambda and p
> covmat = solve(mNull@opt$hessian)
> covmat[1,2]/(covmat[1,1]*covmat[2,2])^0.5
[1] -0.939637

Do you have any advice how to proceed in such a case? Does this mean that the data I obtained in the field is not "enough" to successfully use pcount to estimate abundances?
Is there any other approach that I could follow to estimate abundances, that would work with my data?
My goal is to estimate abundances in the 4 different habitat types and (together with the specific areas of the different habitat types) get an estimate for overall population size.

Thanks a lot!

Markus

Hi Markus,

I agree with Tim that the rain covariate is a bit worrying. Have you tried fitting a model with rain converted to a binary covariate (no/yes or 0/1)? That would be my next move, and then check to see if the predicted detection probabilities are still very high, just to rule out separation as an issue in the model fit.

Ken
